about: Low-level design (object-oriented design + machine coding) from scratch to advanced, in Java: OOP → SOLID and clean code → UML → creational, structural and behavioural patterns → concurrency → the 90-minute machine-coding method → classic problems (parking lot, Splitwise, BookMyShow, elevator, LRU, rate limiter) → DDD, TDD and mock interviews. Builds go into your own lld-practice repo, so you finish with a portfolio. Links checked 2026-10-12.

levels.title: OOP foundations in Java
levels.goal: Model real things as clean objects: the base every design builds on.

lessons.title: Classes, objects and encapsulation
lessons.learn: A class bundles state and behaviour; encapsulation hides state behind methods so its rules (invariants) can't be broken from outside.
lessons.build: Model a BankAccount in Java with a private balance, deposit/withdraw that reject invalid amounts, and 3 JUnit tests.
lessons.check: Why should balance be private with methods instead of a public field?

lessons.title: Abstraction and interfaces
lessons.learn: Interfaces describe what something can do, not how. Code against the interface so implementations can change freely.
lessons.build: Define a PaymentMethod interface with Card and UPI implementations, and a Checkout class that only knows the interface.
lessons.check: What changes in Checkout when you add a Wallet payment method?

lessons.title: Inheritance vs composition
lessons.learn: Inheritance is "is-a" and couples you to the parent; composition is "has-a" and is usually more flexible. Prefer composition.
links: Baeldung: Inheritance and composition in Java
lessons.build: Refactor a Bird → FlyingBird → Penguin inheritance mess into composition with a FlyBehaviour field.
lessons.check: Give one sign that inheritance is the wrong tool?

lessons.title: Polymorphism, equality and immutable values
lessons.learn: Polymorphism lets one call do the right thing per type. Correct equals/hashCode and immutable value objects prevent subtle bugs in maps and sets.
lessons.build: Write a Money record with currency checks, use it as a HashMap key, and prove equal amounts match in a test.
lessons.check: Why must objects used as map keys be immutable?

levels.title: SOLID and clean code
levels.goal: Write code that is easy to change: the principles interviewers probe.

lessons.title: Single responsibility and open/closed
lessons.learn: SRP: one reason to change per class. OCP: add behaviour by adding code, not editing working code.
links: DigitalOcean: SOLID, the first five principles
lessons.build: Split an InvoiceService that calculates, prints and emails by responsibility, then add a new tax rule without editing existing classes.
lessons.check: What is a "reason to change" in SRP?

lessons.title: Liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion
lessons.learn: Subtypes must keep the parent's promises; prefer small interfaces; depend on abstractions and inject dependencies.
lessons.build: Find a fat interface in your own code (or a sample), split it, and inject dependencies through constructors.
lessons.check: How does dependency inversion make code testable?

lessons.title: DRY, KISS, YAGNI and naming
lessons.learn: Remove real duplication, keep it simple, don't build for imaginary futures, and name things for the reader.
lessons.build: Review one Level Up server file: rename 5 unclear names and delete one premature abstraction.
lessons.check: When is duplicating code better than abstracting it?

lessons.title: Code smells and refactoring
lessons.learn: Smells (long method, feature envy, primitive obsession…) point to design problems; small, tested refactorings fix them safely.
lessons.build: Pick 3 smells in a sample project and refactor each while keeping the tests green.
lessons.check: Name a refactoring that fixes primitive obsession?

lessons.title: Checkpoint: design-review your own code
lessons.learn: Reviewing design is a skill: look at responsibilities, coupling, naming and tests, then suggest the smallest useful change.
links: Google engineering practices: what to look for in a review
lessons.build: Write a one-page SOLID review of one Level Up module (what's good + 3 improvements) and apply one of them.
lessons.check: Which SOLID principle does your chosen module break most, and why?

levels.title: UML and modelling
levels.goal: Turn a problem statement into entities, relationships and flows before coding.

lessons.title: From requirements to entities
lessons.learn: Nouns become candidate classes, verbs become methods. Find the core entities, their data and their responsibilities.
lessons.build: For a library system, list the entities, attributes and responsibilities from a 10-line problem statement.
lessons.check: How do you decide whether something is a class or just an attribute?

lessons.title: Class diagrams and relationships
lessons.learn: Association, aggregation, composition, dependency and multiplicity: the vocabulary of every LLD answer.
lessons.build: Draw the library class diagram in Mermaid inside a README, with multiplicities and composition vs aggregation.
lessons.check: What's the difference between aggregation and composition?

lessons.title: Sequence and state diagrams
lessons.learn: Sequence diagrams show who calls whom over time; state diagrams show an object's lifecycle.
lessons.build: Draw the sequence for "borrow a book" and a state diagram for a Book (available → borrowed → overdue → returned).
lessons.check: When is a state diagram more useful than a sequence diagram?

levels.title: Creational patterns
levels.goal: Create objects without hard-wiring concrete classes.

lessons.title: Singleton (and why to be careful)
lessons.learn: One instance, global access. Easy to misuse: hidden dependencies and hard tests. Know the thread-safe versions.
lessons.build: Implement a thread-safe lazy Singleton (holder idiom) and an enum Singleton; write why dependency injection is usually better.
lessons.check: Why are Singletons hard to test?

lessons.title: Factory Method and Abstract Factory
lessons.learn: Let subclasses or factories decide which class to create, so callers depend only on interfaces.
lessons.build: Build a NotificationFactory returning Email/SMS/Push senders, then an abstract factory for light/dark UI widgets.
lessons.check: When would you pick Abstract Factory over Factory Method?

lessons.title: Builder
lessons.learn: Build complex objects step by step, with validation at the end, instead of giant constructors.
lessons.build: Create an HttpRequest builder with a required URL, optional headers and timeout, and validation in build().
lessons.check: What problem does Builder solve that constructors don't?

lessons.title: Prototype + choosing a creational pattern
lessons.learn: Clone configured objects instead of rebuilding them; then learn to match a creation problem to the right pattern.
lessons.build: Clone a configured game Level template with Prototype, and write a 5-line cheat sheet: problem → creational pattern.
lessons.check: Which creational pattern fits "many optional parameters"?

lessons.title: Adapter and Facade
lessons.learn: Adapter makes an incompatible interface fit; Facade gives a simple front door to a complex subsystem.
lessons.build: Wrap a legacy XML weather API behind a JSON WeatherProvider interface (Adapter) and add a TravelFacade over 3 services.
lessons.check: How is an Adapter different from a Facade?

lessons.title: Decorator
lessons.learn: Add responsibilities by wrapping objects, without subclass explosion. Order of wrapping matters.
lessons.build: Stack logging, caching and retry decorators around a DataSource and show that the order changes behaviour.
lessons.check: Why prefer Decorator over many subclasses?

lessons.title: Proxy and Composite
lessons.learn: Proxy controls access (lazy loading, caching, security); Composite treats single items and groups the same way.
lessons.build: Build a lazy-loading ImageProxy and a file-system Composite (File/Folder) that computes total size.
lessons.check: Name two real uses of Proxy?

lessons.title: Bridge and Flyweight
lessons.learn: Bridge separates an abstraction from its implementation; Flyweight shares common state to save memory.
lessons.build: Separate Shape from Renderer with Bridge, then render 10,000 trees sharing Flyweight tree types and compare memory.
lessons.check: What does Flyweight share, and what does it keep per object?

levels.title: Behavioural patterns
levels.goal: Model how objects communicate and change behaviour.

lessons.title: Strategy
lessons.learn: Swap algorithms at runtime behind one interface: the most-used pattern in machine coding rounds.
lessons.build: Swap pricing strategies (regular, festive sale, member) at runtime in a checkout, and add one without touching Checkout.
lessons.check: How does Strategy relate to the open/closed principle?

lessons.title: Observer
lessons.learn: Subjects notify subscribers of changes, keeping them loosely coupled.
lessons.build: Implement a stock ticker where displays subscribe and unsubscribe, then compare it with a simple event bus.
lessons.check: What can go wrong if observers are never unsubscribed?

lessons.title: State and Command
lessons.learn: State moves behaviour into state classes; Command turns requests into objects (queue, log, undo).
lessons.build: Model a vending machine with State classes (idle, has-coin, dispensing) and an undoable Command for a text editor.
lessons.check: When does a switch statement deserve to become the State pattern?

lessons.title: Template Method and Chain of Responsibility
lessons.learn: Template Method fixes an algorithm's skeleton; Chain of Responsibility passes a request along handlers.
lessons.build: Build a request pipeline (auth → rate limit → validation → handler) as a chain, and a report generator with template steps.
lessons.check: How is Chain of Responsibility similar to Express middleware?

lessons.title: Iterator, Visitor and pattern misuse
lessons.learn: Iterator walks collections without exposing them; Visitor adds operations to stable structures. Patterns are tools, not goals.
lessons.build: Write a custom iterator over a tree, and list 3 pattern misuses you've seen with how to avoid them.
lessons.check: When is using a design pattern a bad idea?

levels.title: Concurrency for LLD
levels.goal: Design thread-safe classes: a common machine-coding twist.

lessons.title: Threads, synchronized and visibility
lessons.learn: Race conditions, synchronized blocks, volatile and atomics: what each guarantees.
lessons.build: Make a counter thread-safe three ways (synchronized, AtomicInteger, LongAdder) and benchmark 8 threads.
lessons.check: What does volatile guarantee, and what doesn't it?

lessons.title: Locks, executors and concurrent collections
lessons.learn: Use thread pools instead of raw threads, ReentrantLock when you need more control, and concurrent collections for shared maps and queues.
lessons.build: Process 1,000 tasks with an ExecutorService and a ConcurrentHashMap, plus one ReentrantLock-protected resource.
lessons.check: Why is ConcurrentHashMap better than a synchronized HashMap under load?

lessons.title: Producer–consumer and deadlocks
lessons.learn: Bounded queues decouple producers from consumers; deadlocks need four conditions, so break one of them.
lessons.build: Build a bounded BlockingQueue pipeline, then reproduce a deadlock with two locks and fix it with lock ordering.
lessons.check: What are the four conditions for a deadlock?

lessons.title: Checkpoint: thread-safe LRU cache
lessons.learn: The classic: a HashMap plus a doubly linked list gives O(1) get and put; then make it safe for concurrent use.
lessons.build: Implement an LRU cache (HashMap + doubly linked list), pass LeetCode 146, then make it thread-safe and test with 8 threads.
lessons.check: Which operations in your LRU cache need a lock, and why?

levels.title: The machine-coding method
levels.goal: Deliver a working, extensible design in 90 minutes.

lessons.title: The 90-minute framework
lessons.learn: Clarify requirements (5 min) → entities and relationships (10) → interfaces (10) → core code (50) → demo, tests and extensions (15). Working code beats perfect diagrams.
lessons.build: Write your own one-page machine-coding checklist and keep it at the top of your lld-practice repo.
lessons.check: What should you clarify before writing any code?

lessons.title: Practice: parking lot
lessons.learn: The most-asked LLD problem: floors, spot types, tickets, pricing and payments.
lessons.build: Timebox 90 minutes: parking lot with floors, spot types, tickets, a pricing strategy and an in-memory repository; commit it.
lessons.check: How would you add EV charging spots without rewriting?

lessons.title: Practice: Snake and Ladder
lessons.learn: A game problem that tests clean rules, configuration and turn handling.
lessons.build: Build Snake & Ladder with a configurable board, players and a dice strategy in 60 minutes, with tests for win detection.
lessons.check: Where did you put the game rules, and why there?

lessons.title: Code quality under time pressure
lessons.learn: Interviewers judge readability and extensibility: clear names, small methods, interfaces at the boundaries, no God class, a few tests.
links: Google engineering practices: what to look for in a review
lessons.build: Score your parking lot code 1–5 on correctness, SOLID, naming, tests and extensibility, then fix the lowest score.
lessons.check: What would you skip when time runs out, and what would you never skip?

levels.title: Classic LLD problems
levels.goal: Solve the problems product companies ask most.

lessons.title: Splitwise (expense sharing)
lessons.learn: Users, groups, split types and debt simplification: tests modelling and correctness with money.
lessons.build: Implement users, groups, equal/exact/percent splits and simplify-debts, with unit tests for each split type.
lessons.check: How do you keep balances correct when a split doesn't divide evenly?

lessons.title: BookMyShow (seat booking)
lessons.learn: Theatres, shows, seats and bookings, with the hard part: concurrent seat selection.
lessons.build: Model theatres, shows, seats and bookings, and prevent double booking with a seat lock that expires.
lessons.check: How do you stop two users booking the same seat at the same time?

lessons.title: Elevator system
lessons.learn: Requests, directions and scheduling: a favourite for State and Strategy.
lessons.build: Design elevators with requests, direction and a scheduling strategy (nearest car), and simulate 3 elevators.
lessons.check: Which pattern lets you swap the scheduling algorithm?

lessons.title: Rate limiter and logger
lessons.learn: Token bucket vs sliding window behind one interface; a logger with levels and pluggable outputs.
lessons.build: Implement token-bucket and sliding-window rate limiters behind one interface, and a logger with levels and pluggable sinks.
lessons.check: Token bucket or sliding window: which one allows bursts?

lessons.title: Food delivery order flow
lessons.learn: Restaurants, carts, order states and delivery assignment: State + Strategy together.
lessons.build: Model a Swiggy-style flow (restaurant, cart, order states, delivery-partner assignment strategy) with State and Strategy.
lessons.check: In which states can an order be cancelled, and which class enforces that?

lessons.title: Checkpoint: your LLD portfolio repo
lessons.learn: Five well-documented solutions show design skill better than fifty half-done ones.
lessons.build: Publish an lld-practice repo with 5 solved problems, each with a README: requirements, a Mermaid class diagram, how to run the tests.
lessons.check: Which problem shows your design skills best, and why?

levels.title: Advanced LLD and interviews
levels.goal: Design for change, test it, and explain trade-offs like a senior engineer.

lessons.title: Domain-driven design essentials
lessons.learn: Entities, value objects, aggregates and bounded contexts: the language for modelling complex business logic.
lessons.build: Identify entities, value objects and aggregates in Level Up's referrals hub and write down the aggregate boundaries.
lessons.check: What is an aggregate root responsible for?

lessons.title: Designing for testability (TDD)
lessons.learn: Red → green → refactor. Writing the test first pushes you towards small, decoupled designs.
lessons.build: TDD a small feature (coupon rules) red → green → refactor, committing after each step.
lessons.check: How did writing the test first change your design?

lessons.title: Extensibility with events
lessons.learn: Events let you add features (notifications, analytics) without touching core classes.
links: Martin Fowler: What do you mean by "event-driven"?
lessons.build: Make your Splitwise solution emit events (ExpenseAdded) and add a notification plugin without changing the core classes.
lessons.check: Which of Fowler's event-driven patterns did you use?

lessons.title: Mock LLD interview
lessons.learn: Practise thinking aloud: clarify, model, code, and handle follow-ups about extensions and concurrency.
lessons.build: Do a timed mock on an unseen problem (a friend or the Level Up mentor as interviewer) and write down what you'd improve.
lessons.check: What follow-up question about your design was hardest to answer?
